docs.title: Error faced  Pod status: CrashLoopBackOff
docs.text:
Kubernetes starts your container, it crashes/exits, and Kubelet keeps trying to restart it, but each time it fails again, so Kubernetes backs off (waits longer and longer) before the next restart.

RCA - Got this error coz the image didn't supported the same architecture.

Solution: got into the docker hub of it and found the right multi arch image and updated the pod file.

docs.title: Concept of labels and Selectors
docs.text:
Labels are key/value pairs that are attached to objects, such as pods. Labels are intended to be used to specify identifying attributes of objects that are meaningful and relevant to users.

Selectors are used to filter a list of resources based on their labels. They allow users to select a subset of resources that match certain criteria.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
--> service is a long running object with long stable running port.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
    #Unique key of the service
    name: flettman-webapp-service
spec:
    # This defines which pods are gonna be represented by this service
    # The service becomes a endpoint to access the pods / or for other # # services to access the pods
    selector:
        app: webapp

    ports:
    - name: http
      protocol: TCP
      port: 80            # Port on which the service is exposed
      targetPort: 80     # Port on the pod to which the traffic is 
      nodePort: 30080  # Port on each node to expose the service (only for NodePort type)

    type: NodePort #second P is capital

docs.title: replicaSet in kubernetes or rs
docs.text: 1. It is an extra piece of configuration to ensure that the Kubernetes pods are always running for the desired number of replicas.

docs.title: Points to remember
docs.text:
• ReplicaSet is a higher-level abstraction that manages multiple instances of a pod.
  • it has 3 new keys
    • template: pod template that defines the pod's configuration (inside spec)
    • selector: label selector to identify the pods managed by the ReplicaSet (match labels for which we are applying pod)
    • replicas: number of desired pod instances
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: ReplicaSet
metadata: 
    name: webapp
spec:
    replicas: 1
    selector:
        matchLabels:
            app: webapp #this  should match
    template:
        metadata:
            labels:
                app: webapp #this  should match
        spec:
            containers:
            - name: webapp
              image: nginx

docs.title: Note
docs.text:
1. Pods created by ReplicaSet will have a unique suffix added to their names for identification. like webapp-xxxxx
  2. use the scale command to scale up or down yaml k scale --replicas=

docs.title: Testing it
docs.text:
1. I deleted all the pods using k delete po --all
  2. It swapped to 0/1 pods
  3. It spawned the new pods with new suffix within seconds

docs.title: Deployments
docs.text:
• A deployment is a Kubernetes resource that provides declarative updates to applications.
  • It manages the creation and scaling of Pods, ensuring that the desired number of replicas are running at any given time.
  • Deployments are commonly used for stateless applications, allowing for easy updates and rollbacks.
  • Similar to ReplicaSet but with rolling updates and rollback, providing zero downtime for application deployments.

docs.title: Nothing but the glorified ReplicaSet
docs.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: 
    name: webapp
spec:
    replicas: 1
    selector:
        matchLabels:
            app: webapp # this should match
    template:
        metadata:
            labels:
                app: webapp # this should match
        spec:
            containers:
            - name: webapp
              image: nginx

docs.title: Revision
docs.text:
• Every time you change the Pod template inside a Deployment, Kubernetes creates a new ReplicaSet, and that creates a new revision.
  • Triggers a new revision:
  • Changing image (nginx:1.19 → nginx:1.20)
  • Changing env vars
  • Changing labels in pod template
  • Changing resource limits
  • Does NOT trigger revision:
  • Scaling replicas count
  • Changing annotations on Deployment metadata

docs.title: Rollout
docs.text: Rollout is how Kubernetes replaces old Pods with new Pods during a Deployment update.

docs.title: 1. Add the nodeName property
docs.text:
This only works at the time of Pod creation.

nodeName: <node-name>

Sample resource YAML:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx
spec:
  containers:
  - image: nginx
    name: nginx
  nodeName: node01

docs.title: 2. Add the nodeSelector property
docs.text:
This works at the time of creation and after the Pod is created.

nodeSelector:
  <label-key>: <label-value>

docs.title: 3. Send a binding request to the kube-apiserver
docs.text:
This binds the Pod to a specific node.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Binding
metadata:
  name: <pod-name>
  namespace: <namespace-name>
target:
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Node
  name: <node-name>

docs.title: Taints and Tolerations
docs.text: Taints and tolerations are a flexible way to steer Pods away from nodes or evict Pods that should not be running.

docs.title: 1. Taints
docs.text:
Taints are applied to nodes and repel a set of Pods. Tolerations are applied to Pods and allow them to schedule onto nodes with matching taints, although they are not required.

By default, no Pods have tolerations, so they can only be scheduled onto nodes that do not have taints.

kubectl taint nodes <node-name> key=value:taint-effect

docs.title: Types of taint effects
docs.text:
• NoSchedule: Pods that do not tolerate this taint will not be scheduled on the node, but Pods already running on the node remain.
  • PreferNoSchedule: Kubernetes tries to avoid placing a Pod that does not tolerate the taint on the node, but it is not a hard requirement.
  • NoExecute: Pods that do not tolerate this taint are evicted from the node if they are already running there, and are not scheduled on the node if they are not already running there.

docs.title: 2. Tolerations
docs.text:
Tolerations are applied to Pods and allow them to schedule onto nodes with matching taints.

tolerations:
- key: "key1"
  operator: "Equal"
  value: "value1"
  effect: "NoSchedule"

docs.title: Use cases of taints and tolerations
docs.text:
1. Dedicated Nodes: Restrict nodes to specific workloads using taints and tolerations. Use node labels + node affinity to ensure those Pods run only on dedicated nodes.
  2. Special Hardware (e.g., GPUs): Taint GPU nodes to keep unrelated Pods away. Pods requiring GPUs use matching tolerations and resource requests to schedule there.
  3. Taint-based Evictions: Automatically evict Pods when nodes experience problems, depending on the taint effect and toleration settings.
kubectl taint nodes controlplane dedicated=special:NoSchedule-

CKA tip: The trailing - removes the taint. Replace dedicated=special with the actual taint shown on your node.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• NoSchedule: New Pods without matching tolerations will not schedule.
  • PreferNoSchedule: Kubernetes tries to avoid scheduling Pods without matching tolerations.
  • NoExecute: Evicts existing Pods without matching tolerations and prevents new ones from scheduling.

docs.title: NodeSelector
docs.text:
NodeSelector is a 1:1 mapping between node labels and the pod's nodeSelector. If the node has the same label key-value pair as in the pod spec, the pod is scheduled on that node.

Label the node with a key-value pair and use the same key-value pair in the pod spec to schedule the pod onto that node.

k label nodes <node-name> <label-key>=<label-value>

Then add the following to the pod:

nodeSelector:
  <label-key>: <label-value>

docs.title: static Pods
docs.text:
when no master is there

there is no scheduling of pods on the node. The node will be in NotReady state and no pods will be scheduled on it.so kubelet can create pods and read the pod file and create the pod from this directory /etc/kubernetes/manifests. The kubelet will create the pod and run it on the node. This is called static pod. Static pods are managed directly by the kubelet daemon on a specific node, without the need for a Kubernetes control plane. This is ony for pods not for deployments, replica sets, or other higher-level abstractions.

  1. to see the pods bash docker ps -a

docs.title: Troubleshooting Guide
docs.text: Common Kubernetes issues and their solutions.

docs.title: 📘 Issues
docs.text:
• Resource name may not be empty
  • ReplicaSet won't touch existing pods
  • Why Pod didn't come back

docs.title: Why did you have to delete the Pod manually?
docs.text:
Sequence you described:

ReplicaSet created with template using image tag ...release0-5. → Pod comes up fine.

You delete that Pod with kubectl delete pod . → ReplicaSet notices it has 0/1 Pods and creates a new Pod from the same template ✅

You break the template (wrong image name). → New Pod is created, but it goes to ImagePullBackOff.

You fix the image name in the ReplicaSet YAML and run kubectl apply -f workload.yaml. → ReplicaSet object is updated, but the bad Pod is still there.

ReplicaSet sees: “I should have 1 replica; I already have 1 Pod (even if it’s failing), so my job is done.” → It does not delete or recreate that Pod.

You manually delete the Pod. → ReplicaSet now sees 0/1 Pods and creates a new one — this time using the corrected template, so it works.

👉 Key idea: A ReplicaSet does not update existing Pods when you change the template. It only ensures the count of Pods. If the count is satisfied, it won’t touch running / failing Pods.

To force new Pods with the updated template you must either:

delete the old Pods:

kubectl delete pod

docs.title: or all pods of that RS:
docs.text:
kubectl delete pods -l app=webapp

OR change spec.replicas (e.g. scale to 0 then back to 1).

For automatic rollouts when the template changes, Kubernetes uses a Deployment, which internally creates new ReplicaSets and gradually replaces Pods. That’s why for “normal apps” we use Deployment instead of raw ReplicaSet

docs.title: RCA: “resource name may not be empty”
Issue:
docs.text:
kubectl apply -f <file> returned: 

error: resource name may not be empty.

docs.title: Root Cause:
docs.text: The metadata field in the YAML manifest was misspelled. Because metadata was incorrect, Kubernetes could not read metadata.name, resulting in an empty resource name.

docs.title: How the issue was identified:
docs.text:
• The error referenced Resource=pods, meaning Kubernetes parsed the file as a Pod manifest.
  • Pods require metadata.name.
  • The error persisted even after renaming the file, which pointed to malformed YAML rather than content type.
  • This strongly suggested Kubernetes could not find metadata.name, which typically happens when metadata: is misspelled or incorrectly indented.
  • You confirmed that metadata was indeed misspelled.

docs.title: Impact:
docs.text:
• Kubernetes was unable to create or update the resource.
  • Deployment was blocked until YAML was corrected.

docs.title: Fix:
docs.text: • Corrected the spelling of metadata: and ensured a valid metadata.name exists.

docs.title: Prevention:
docs.text:
• Use kubectl apply --dry-run=client to catch manifest issues early.
  • Enable YAML validation in your editor (VSCode Kubernetes/YAML extensions).

docs.title: Why your pod didn’t come back
docs.text:
1. The pod labels do not match the Service selector

    • Ensure that the labels defined in your pod specification match the selector criteria specified in your Service definition. If they do not match, the Service will not be able to route traffic to the pod.

    kubectl get svc -o yaml

    kubectl get pods --show-labels
